Important Information
This Climate Statement (‘Statement’) is prepared for the purposes of Climate-Related Disclosures under 
Part 7A of the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 (FMCA) and the External Reporting Board’s Climate 
Standards (NZ CS), for the year ended 31 March 2024. It has been prepared for our primary users, being 
Toi Foundation as our sole shareholder, and existing and potential customers, lenders and other creditors. 
The Statement contains climate-related and other forward-looking statements and metrics, including 
climate related scenarios, transition planning, assumptions, climate projections, forecasts, statements 
of TSB’s future intentions, estimates and judgements which are not and should not be considered 
guarantees, predictions or forecasts of TSB’s present and future strategies, future climate-related 
outcomes or financial performance. These statements are subject to known and unknown risks, inherent 
uncertainties, limitations around inputs and available data, and other factors, many of which are beyond 
the Bank’s control. Readers are cautioned not to place undue reliance on such statements in light of the 
significant uncertainty in climate metrics and modelling that limit the extent they are useful for decision-
making, and the many underlying risks and assumptions may cause actual outcomes to differ materially. 
The risks and opportunities described here and our transition plan objectives may not eventuate or may 
be more or less significant than anticipated. There are many factors that could cause TSB’s actual results, 
performance or achievement of our objectives to differ materially from that described, including economic 
and technological viability, as well as climatic, government, consumer, and market factors outside of TSB’s 
control.
This report reflects TSB’s best estimate and current understanding of future climate related events, risks, 
opportunities, impacts and strategies as at 16 July 2024. TSB has sought to provide a reasonable basis for 
forward-looking statements and is committed to progressing our response to climate-related risks and 
opportunities over time but is constrained by the novel and developing nature of this subject matter.  We 
are committed to progressing our response to climate-related risks and opportunities over time, and 
to report our progress each year, but we caution reliance on aspects of this report which is necessarily 
subject to the caveats above. While we have prepared the information in this report based on our current 
knowledge, understanding and in good faith, we reserve the right to change our view in the future. 
Reporting entity: The Statement covers TSB Bank Limited only. TSB Bank Limited has no subsidiaries. It has 
one shareholder, Toi Foundation Holdings Limited, a 100% subsidiary of Toi Foundation. References to 
‘TSB’, ‘the Bank’, ‘we’, ‘us’ and ‘our’ mean TSB Bank Limited. 
For detailed information on our financial performance, please refer to the TSB Disclosure Statements and 
Annual Report, available on the TSB website at www.tsb.co.nz.

Kia ora koutou and welcome to TSB’s 2024 Climate Statement.
Climate change is one of the most important challenges the world faces today: Temperatures are rising, 
weather patterns are changing, and here in Aotearoa we have seen firsthand the devastating impacts of 
the increase in extreme weather events.
TSB has a proud 172-year history of growing, adapting, and pushing boundaries, and it is this heritage that 
drives us forward to ensure we are doing our part to combat climate change.
This Climate Statement is our first formal step in responding to these challenges, outlining our strategic 
approach to managing climate related risks, our sustainability policy development, our emissions 
measurements and targets, and our timeframes for reduction.
We know there is much more work to do to achieve our sustainability and climate change goals, but we 
are proud of these important first steps and we are determined to continue to build from here. 
Ngā mihi nui,
                                                 
Mark Darrow

Responsibility
Under TSB’s Board Charter, the Board has the responsibility to set the direction of TSB’s response to 
climate change and oversee climate-related risks and opportunities.
Description of oversight
The Board Risk Committee (BRC) is a sub-committee of the Board, which meets quarterly and under 
its charter is responsible for monitoring climate-related risks. Sustainability, including climate-related 
risk, is a Material Risk to TSB. The Enterprise Risk Management Framework sets out the oversight and 
reporting of Material Risks, including BRC’s oversight. BRC carries this out through review of information, 
recommendations, and reporting provided by management, notably by the Executive Risk Committee 
(ERC)1 via a quarterly Material Risks report. Material Risks reports are then presented to the Board once 
they have been reviewed by the BRC.

The Board reviewed initial reporting on climate-related risks and opportunities during FY24. Climate-
related risks and opportunities have been a standing agenda item at quarterly Board meetings since 
September 2023 and were the subject of Board discussions at meetings prior to then.
Key climate-related inputs to the Board are:
•	
Material Risks report (quarterly from Executive Risk Committee)
•	
Climate Change impact on Strategy report (annual) – from FY25 onwards (from GM People & Strategy)
•	
Metrics dashboard (including Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions and tracking vs targets) – quarterly 
from FY25 onwards (from Chief Financial Officer)
•	
Annual Climate Statement (from Chief Financial Officer)
The Board has received reporting on climate matters, but climate-related risks and opportunities have 
not yet been incorporated into TSB’s strategy, as considered and set out by the Board in the TSB 2030 
Strategy. Climate-related risks and opportunities will be more fully incorporated into the development and 
oversight of TSB strategy from FY25 onwards.
To support the above processes, the Sustainability Working Group (SWG) has been established in FY24 
to provide support to the Board in an advisory capacity in relation to wider sustainability issues. The 
SWG comprises two Board members and an external Sustainability expert as group Chair. It held its first 
meeting in February 2024 and will continue its work as we build TSB’s sustainability maturity. The SWG 
played a key role in developing the Sustainability Policy, which the Board approved in June 2024. The 
Sustainability Policy includes a commitment to ensure our sustainability framework acknowledges and 
aligns with Te Ao Māori.
TSB is currently developing our processes to further inform the Board regarding climate-related 
opportunities. We expect these to be in place during FY25.

TSB’s Board reviewed the following metrics for GHG gross emissions (metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent 
(tCO2e)) during FY24:
•	
Scope 1

•

The Board also reviewed the following intensity metrics during FY24: Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions per 
FTE and per $m of net operating income. These metrics have been included in ad-hoc reporting during 
the establishment of GHG emissions measurement in the current financial year, and will be included in 
quarterly dashboard reporting, together with Scope 3 operational emissions, from the Chief Financial 
Officer to the Board from FY25 onwards to monitor progress and achievement. The Board does not yet 
receive reporting on Scope 3 financed emissions as they are not measured yet by TSB (FY25 activity). Our 
measurement of Scope 3 operational emissions excludes sources estimated to be below a de minimis 
threshold (and therefore not material to our GHG emissions).
The Board is responsible for the approval of TSB’s GHG emissions targets. The Board Audit Committee 
(BAC) has supported the Board by reviewing TSB’s GHG targets and the associated reduction pathways to 
achieve the stated targets, with support from the SWG.
GHG emissions measurement of TSB’s Scope 1 and 2 and Scope 3 operational emissions, and initial 
reduction targets for Scope 1 and 2 emissions, have been established by the Board in FY24. The 
achievement of GHG-related performance metrics is not currently incorporated into TSB’s remuneration 
policies. We intend to review this in FY25, with the outcome of the review being actioned from FY26 at the 
earliest.

TSB continues to develop our processes to consider climate opportunities and reporting.

Current Climate-related Impacts
Climate change leads to increasing risks of extreme weather events and more gradually progressive 
impacts such as sea level rise and ocean acidification. These are referred to as physical risks, and are 
typically divided into:
•	
Acute – the risk of impacts from extreme weather events; and 
•	
Chronic – the risk of gradual impacts. 
Transition risks arise as an economy takes steps to mitigate physical risks and progress towards lower 
emissions. For example, low emissions policies can lead to increased costs for businesses and households, 
and societal preferences are shifting towards more sustainable businesses, which risks creating stranded 
assets and unprofitable businesses.
Potential impacts associated with physical and transition risks can also lead to climate-related 
opportunities for TSB. (See Appendix 1 for further background information). 
TSB has no current material climate-related physical or transition impacts for the year to 31 March 2024. 
Consequently, there were no material financial impacts for this period.
Physical impacts
TSB does not consider that it has experienced material physical impacts to our credit portfolio as a result 
of climate-related events due to our insurance and equity requirements for borrowers, customers’ existing 
equity, and local and national government policy (mitigating factors).
Credit level
This includes the physical impacts of the January and February 2023 flooding events and cyclone, which 
are likely related to climate change. Some of our customers were impacted by these events (for example, 
property damage from flooding) but the mitigating factors noted above were sufficient to prevent TSB 
experiencing a material credit impact in FY24.
Organisational level 
We provided support to our customers who were impacted by these events, but the operational costs 
associated with our response were not material to our FY24 result. There were no other material 
operational impacts from those events either as TSB buildings (where owned by TSB) are fully insured, and 
business interruption processes provide for primary customer services online and by phone. Some of our 
branch locations were impacted (for example, branch access difficulties) but the mitigating factors noted 
here prevented the operational impact being material in FY24. Additionally, there were no significant IT 
service interruptions or supply chain impacts due to the above events, including from damage to data 
centres. 
Transition impacts 
TSB has not yet experienced any material adverse or positive credit or operational impacts from the 
transition to a low emissions economy. 
Opportunities
We have reviewed areas for potential resource efficiency savings, emissions reductions and climate 
resilience, as well as new products to assist customers’ reduction of environmental impact (see Climate-
related risks and opportunities on page 17).

Scenario Analysis: TSB Climate Scenarios 
The goal of TSB’s scenario analysis is to be aware of and prepared for what realistically may occur in the 
world as a result of climate change – to promote resilience under plausible future climate states. 
The scope of TSB’s scenario analysis is set by the focal question: ‘How could climate change plausibly affect 
our business model and strategy through the creation of risks and opportunities?’ To answer this TSB 
has chosen to utilise the banking sector scenario analysis provided by New Zealand Banking Association 
(NZBA) (Te Rangapū Pēke) and focus on the parts of that analysis that are applicable to TSB’s business 
model and strategy. The sector analysis is based on three climate reference scenarios published by the 
Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), tailored to New Zealand circumstances:
Orderly Transition
A future world where collective action is taken towards a low carbon 
global economy (1.5°C scenario)
Too Little Too Late
Fragmented and delayed transition to a low carbon economy between 
New Zealand (early mover) and the rest of the world (fossil-fuelled 
development to mid-century) (Other scenario)
Hothouse
Minimal action towards a low carbon global transition, increasing levels 
of social, economic, and environmental degradation (>3°C scenario)
Details of the time horizons used are set out in the table on the next page. When considering the 
narratives for each scenario, TSB has conducted an analysis of our business model, considered our value 
chain and focused on our material customer sectors of residential and commercial property lending, and 
in geographical locations relevant to TSB. In addition, we have maintained awareness of agriculture as a 
lending category and other sectors of the economy as employers of mortgage customers and relevant to 
business lending.
TSB has selected the NZBA sector level scenario analysis because it:
•	
Provides consistency in banking sector disclosure comparisons.
•	
Is developed by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) as relevant to the banking 
sector.
•	
Has scenarios which meet Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) criteria of being 
plausible, distinctive, consistent, relevant and challenging.
•	
Bases scenarios on IPCC global reference scenarios and applying New Zealand climate parameters 
NIWA RCPs 2.6, 4.5 and 8.5 (lowest to highest emissions), and Climate Change Commission pathways, 
provides additional plausibility and local relevance. 
Further description of the three scenarios and the assumptions which underlie them is set out in 
Appendix 2 – TSB Scenario Narratives, along with the possible physical and transition impacts which may 
arise under each scenario.

Scenario Analysis Processes and Governance 
We are building capability in scenario analysis. For this first disclosure, scenario analysis has been 
conducted as a standalone exercise with input across the bank. The project team that conducted the 
exercise reports to the Climate-related Disclosures project steering committee that includes members 
of the ELT and the senior leadership team and the Board has reviewed a summary of the scenarios and 
outputs. 
We engaged Mosaic to provide support for our scenario analysis processes (www.mosaicfsi.com/
sustainability). No external partners or stakeholders were involved in this first entity level analysis, 
although industry peers’ and climate science and data providers’ contributions, amongst others, were 
sought as part of the sector level scenario analysis. 
TSB has not conducted our own modelling to produce the scenario narratives but utilised those 
provided in the NZBA analysis. TSB modelling, using physical risk data sourced from an external provider 
(CoreLogic), has been performed for assessment of scope and size of physical risks – see TSB Climate-
related Risks and Opportunities below and the Risk Management section (page 24). 
TSB intends to conduct an annual review of our scenarios to ensure they continue to meet regulatory 
requirements and contribute to effectively assessing climate-related risks and opportunities and the 
resilience of TSB’s business model and strategy. Additionally, we expect to rerun scenario analysis when 
any sector level updates are issued or we become aware of material changes to drivers or outcomes in 
these narratives.
We remain focussed on continuous improvement and intend to integrate consideration of scenario 
analysis more fully into the strategy process, and include external partners and stakeholders in future.

TSB Climate-related Risks and Opportunities
TSB’s climate-related risk management processes have identified multiple risks based on the scenario 
analysis performed above. This disclosure reports on material risks as assessed using the TSB 
Sustainability Risk Assessment Matrix (SRAM, see Risk Management (page 24)). To be considered material 
for this disclosure, a risk must be assessed as ‘High’ or above. These material risks are shown in the 
applicable time horizon and may be from any of the three scenarios. This is to support resilience actions 
being both timely and based on plausible scenarios, so TSB can be prepared for any material risk. 
Figure 4: TSB’s risk management process to determine material risks 
Time horizons 
TSB applies the same time horizons as for scenario analysis: short-term (around 2030); medium term 
(around 2050); and long-term (2080+). TSB’s current strategic planning and capital deployment horizon is 
out to 2030, being the short term in our climate-related time horizons. We intend to review this as part of 
our maturing approach to climate risk. 
Capital deployment
Since June 2023, associated climate-related risks and opportunities are considered by the Benefits and 
Investment Committee (management-level committee) in respect of strategic programmes and projects 
at TSB as part of funding decision-making processes. This covers only part of TSB’s capital deployment 
and funding decision-making processes, so we intend to expand the consideration of such risks and 
opportunities within those processes at TSB as part of maturing our approach.

understand the future will be different as a result of the impacts of climate change. Our business model

Climate-related risk awareness and knowledge
We acknowledge understanding the complex nature of climate-related risk is critical to effective 
management. In the first quarter of FY25, we have been building awareness of climate change and 
associated risk across TSB. In the remainder of FY25, we expect to launch training to provide those that 
directly manage climate-related risk as part of their role at TSB with additional knowledge and skills to 
enable this. 
Value chain
TSB has considered our entire value chain in our risk management processes for climate-related risks (see 
value chain diagram in Strategy section (page 12)). TSB measured all our operational emissions (Scope 1, 
Scope 2, and Scope 3 operational emissions) in the FY24 GHG emissions assessment, which has informed 
our assessment of operational risk from climate change across the business. Once our Scope 3 financed 
emissions are measured in FY25, we expect to consider those emissions when we next review the climate-
related risks relevant to the bank.
Frequency
We review the risk assessment of all risks in the climate-related risk inventory annually and whenever new 
climate scenario analysis is performed (see Strategy section (page 14)). Outside of this it is the responsibility 
of business units as risk owners to ensure risk assessments reflect all currently available information.
Prioritisation
TSB’s assessment of climate-related risks spans the short to long term. While all our Material Risk categories 
are given priority, TSB understands the importance of managing climate-related risks that extend beyond 
the typical time horizons for risk management. To support this, we apply an approach to climate-related 
risk materiality that considers risks associated with the plausible scenarios on an equal footing. This 
means climate-related risks that are assessed as ‘High’ or above in any of the three climate scenarios are 
considered as material risks for the development of action plans regardless of the time horizon.
Integration into existing ERMF
Risks at TSB are managed within the Enterprise Risk Management Framework (ERMF). We have begun 
integrating climate-related risk into the ERMF over the last two financial years and continue to make 
progress in this exercise. 
While we continue to integrate climate-related risk into the ERMF, we have used a project approach for risk 
management of climate-related risks as an interim measure in FY24 whilst we build on-going capability.
Climate-related risk is currently being integrated into the ERMF as follows:
•	
Climate-related risk is incorporated into risk governance structures: the Board and Board Risk 
Committee (BRC) have express oversight obligations for climate risks.
•	
To date, climate-related risk has been captured as a bank level Material Risk with a residual risk appetite 
rating of medium, under Sustainability Risk, which is defined as “the risk of reputational or financial loss 
due to failure to recognise or address material existing or emerging environmental or climate-related issues.”
Climate-related risk is managed both as a standalone risk (as above) and as a cross-cutting risk, i.e., within 
existing risk types. Those risk types, particularly financial risk categories of liquidity, funding and capital risk, 
and strategy risk, can be affected by climate risk due to flow-on from impacts on organisational and credit 
risk. TSB is in the process of including these downstream risks in our Sustainability risk assessment and

Our Targets
Target and ambition
TSB is committed to taking steps to contribute to the limiting of global warming, TSB has set absolute  
GHG emissions reduction targets it considers ambitious but realistic. Our Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions 
science-aligned target is a 42% reduction by FY30 from the FY23 emissions baseline. A science-aligned 
target meets SBTi (Science Based Targets Initiative) guidance to contribute to limiting global warming to 
1.5°C above pre-industrial levels but has not necessarily been independently verified by SBTi. We choose 
to align with SBTi because they provide a clearly defined pathway to reduce GHG emissions, helping 
prevent the worst physical impacts of climate change and support business resilience. We have not 
submitted our target to SBTi for formal validation.
We have also set an ambition to reach net zero by 2050 for our Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions, which is 
likely to require some use of offsets, as noted below.
Performance against targets
Our target for FY24 was to reduce our total Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 6% from the FY23 emissions 
baseline. We achieved a 26.2% reduction in those emissions in FY24. We are pleased we have more than 
achieved this target for FY24 but acknowledge this is only the first year of our journey to our FY30 target 
for these emissions, and that by expanding our reporting to include all Scope 3 operational emissions,

reduction of 6% in our Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions each year from FY23.

Our reduction pathways to meet our FY30 target for Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions do not rely on offsets. 
However, our ambition to reach net zero by 2050 for the same emissions is likely to require high quality 
carbon offsets or similar mechanisms for hard to abate emissions and any residual emissions resulting 
from non-renewable energy use from the NZ grid. We expect any required offsets TSB uses will meet 
Toitū’s verification requirements or those required for similar certification.

Now we have completed the measurement of operational Scope 3 GHG emissions in FY24, we expect 
to set appropriate targets for those emissions during FY25 once we understand the potential reduction 
pathways. We plan to set 2030 progress targets for intervening financial years for operational Scope 3 
GHG emissions in FY25. Those progress targets are likely to be a balance of numerical and other targets, 
such as engagement levels with suppliers. Similarly, we expect to consider Scope 3 financed GHG 
emissions targets in FY25 once those emissions have been measured. However, it may be FY26 before

Orderly Transition 1.5°C
Overview
A future world where collective action is taken towards a low carbon global economy.
Description
In this scenario there is collective global climate action taken from the immediate term and the ambitious 
goals of the Paris Agreement are met, with governments worldwide moving forward simultaneously 
towards a low carbon economy. Regulations promoting low carbon products, services and operations, 
such as building energy efficiency standards, and additional industries subject to the Emissions Trading 
Scheme (ETS), are strengthened, and carbon prices rise steadily and significantly in the immediate and 
short term, adding costs to higher emitting industries including construction, transport and energy - all 
further promoting low-carbon producer and customer behaviour change. Consumers are well aware of 
the need to decarbonise the economy and therefore expect products and services, and residential and 
commercial properties, to be low emissions, and for businesses and other organisations to reduce their 
emissions in line with New Zealand and global carbon net zero by 2050. 
From the immediate term and continuing beyond the medium term, technology is steadily but rapidly 
developed to mitigate emissions such as electrification of transport and industry, carbon capture and 
sequestration and resilience (adaptation) measures. Fossil fuels are gradually phased out in favour 
of these low emissions technologies, and global electricity generation shifts towards fully renewable 
sources. In this scenario, the widespread policy support for low emissions technologies reduces reliance 
on afforestation to absorb residual emissions, allowing for greater rates of native afforestation. In the 
long term, policy support is provided for further mitigation actions and greater afforestation in order to 
maintain the net zero status including further emissions for remaining high-emitting sectors and greater 
use of emissions removals (Climate Change Commission, 2021).
As a result of this coordinated and timely action around the world to curb GHG emissions, emissions 
decline from the short term and reach net zero by 2040 in New Zealand (Ministry for the Environment, 
2018. Climate Change Projections for New Zealand: Atmospheric Projections Based on Simulations from 
the IPCC Fifth Assessment, 2nd Edition) and 2050 globally, preventing the worst predicted physical impacts 
of climate change. However, the long-term chronic physical impacts from historic GHG emissions are still 
likely to occur, although to a less severe extent than the other scenarios.

Overview
Fragmented and delayed transition to a low carbon economy between New Zealand (early mover) and the

Description
In this scenario New Zealand transitions to a low carbon economy ahead of the global pace, introducing 
proactive climate action policies and reaching net zero emissions by 2048 (Climate Change Commission,

albeit less emphatically than under the Orderly Transition scenario and there is reluctance to reduce 
emissions in some sectors. New Zealand carbon prices increase at pace with the Orderly Transition 
scenario from the short term to medium term. Before the short term the agriculture sector is subject 
to emissions pricing and the New Zealand government introduces regulations that limit emissions and 
energy consumption of commercial properties. Renewable electricity share, already high in New Zealand, 
continues to grow and almost matches the Orderly Transition scenario in both the short and medium 
term. 
Worldwide action, however, is very limited at first and fossil fuels continue to dominate energy use until 
near to mid-century. There is limited development of low emissions technologies over this time which 
constrains New Zealand’s transition. In this scenario, due to the limited availability of low emission 
technology in New Zealand, afforestation becomes a key tool to achieve net zero by 2050. As a result, 
the demand for unused rural land and less profitable farmland that can be converted into exotic forestry 
increases. Greater global support for low emission technology from the medium term helps to reduce the 
reliance on forestry somewhat. However, the lag in leveraging this technology sees forestry rates continue 
to climb.
Global emissions continue to increase in the immediate and short term. The global transition commences 
around the medium term in reaction to clear physical effects of climate change and awareness of its 
harmful consequences to society, the economy and the environment. From this time global carbon prices 
increase significantly and there is widespread adoption of low emissions technologies. Global emissions 
now begin to decline. Unfortunately, these changes come too late to prevent a number of acute and 
chronic physical climate impacts materialising from the medium term.

Description
Hothouse is the ‘worst-case scenario’ of the three analysed, representing minimal action from the 
immediate to long term towards a low carbon global transition. There are minimal low carbon regulations 
and carbon pricing remains ineffectually low. As a result, there is little behaviour change and a lack of 
technology development and uptake. Fossil fuel use continues increasing as does mass consumption. 
Locally, New Zealand takes a slightly more proactive approach to climate action with existing policies 
such as retention of the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) but with the global inertia there is limited public 
sentiment for substantial change. Action taken therefore is only enough to create a small reduction in 
domestic emissions. Adoption of low emissions technologies, already with only limited availability, largely 
only occurs where this is cost-saving rather than a change in societal expectations and behaviour. There 
continues to be high global demand for meat and dairy products up to the medium term, assisting New 
Zealand livestock farming. Renewable electricity share, already high in New Zealand, grows only very 
slightly, with global share growing but well under the more progressive scenarios. 
In this scenario, the retention of the New Zealand ETS and the high carbon price in the mid-2020s 
continues to generate a financial incentive to plant forests in the short term. In the medium term, the scale 
of forest planting scales back as the focus on meeting carbon budgets is lost but global growth in demand 
helps to provide incentives to expand forests around New Zealand for logging purposes, which sees 
exotic land area expand from 2.1Mha in the short term to 2.8Mha in the medium term (Climate Change 
Commission, 2021).
Despite increasing levels of social, economic and environmental degradation caused by the significantly 
worsening climate by the medium term, there is little shift in social and political traction towards a low 
emissions future.
The impact of these activities and inaction drives emissions higher throughout the remaining 21st 
century leading to significant materialisation of acute and chronic physical risks globally particularly from 
mid-century onwards. Heading into the medium term (the first half of the 21st century), this sees some 
increase in severity of extreme weather, later accompanied by rising sea levels beyond the medium term 
resulting in high physical risk. This threatens coastal developments worldwide, placing pressure on global 
relations. Overall, when considered alongside the Orderly Transition and Too Little Too Late scenarios, this 
scenario represents low transition impacts and a high level of physical impacts.

Appendix 3:
GHG Calculation Methodology
The calculation methodology has been used for quantifying the emissions inventory based on the 
following calculation approach below (unless otherwise stated): 
Emissions  =  activity data  x  emissions factor
Activity data is derived from reports, invoices and data from the relevant data source/supplier and in most 
cases the relevant emission factors are applied to calculate the emissions (some organisations supplied 
actual emissions values). Emission factors and Global Warming Potentials were sourced from the Ministry 
for the Environment NZ publication, Measuring emissions: A guide for organisations, 2023 detailed guide. 
100-year GWPs from IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) have also been used as a preferred approach 
where available. 
Where full source data was unavailable to calculate actual emissions, unit conversion methods were 
applied when calculating activity-based emissions. For example, when calculating emissions from fuel 
usage, actual fuel usage for some vehicles was unavailable. Accordingly, we calculated emissions for those 
vehicles by converting the actual amount spent on fuel into actual fuel usage by using an average fuel cost 
per litre factor. 
Uncertainty has been calculated through using estimates of uncertainty both using the data completeness 
category and the emission factor themselves. The uncertainty values have been sourced from Toitū 
Envirocare. 
There are systems and procedures in place that will ensure applied quantification methodologies will 
continue in future GHG emissions inventories. This supports consistency of GHG emissions measurement 
between different periods.
